title: Why a local minimum is global
objectives: Prove that a local minimum of a convex function on a convex set is global.

screens.title: Where the ball stops
screens.prose: Here is $f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + x$. Drag the start along the curve; the orange path is a ball rolling downhill from it. Try starts on both sides of the hump near $x = 0.17$.

derive.caption: From $x$ = {{fixed(S.x, 2)}} the ball stops at $x$ = {{fixed(values.TEndX, 4)}}, where $f$ = {{fixed(values.TEndY, 4)}}.

screens.question: Start at $x = 1.8$. At what $x$ does the ball stop?

hints.text: Put the start at $x = 1.8$ and read the caption.
It rolls left into the right-hand dip.

feedback.correct: It stops at about 1.1309, with $f \approx -1.0702$. It never sees the deeper dip on the left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read where the orange path ends for a start at 1.8.

byKey.global: $-1.3008$ is the deeper dip, but a start at 1.8 cannot climb the hump to reach it.
byKey.hump: 0.1699 is the hump, a local maximum. The ball rolls away from it.

explain.text: From 1.8 the ball rolls into the dip at $x \approx 1.1309$, with $f \approx -1.0702$. Starts left of the hump at 0.1699 end at $x \approx -1.3008$ instead, where $f \approx -3.5139$.

screens.title: Two resting places
screens.prose: Every start ends at one of two points. At each, no small move lowers $f$: each is a **local minimum**. The lowest value of $f$ anywhere is the **global minimum**.
screens.question: Tap the global minimum.

hints.text: The lower one, on the left, is the global minimum.

feedback.correct: The left point, with $f \approx -3.5139$, is global. The right one is only local.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the lower of the two resting points.

byKey.local: That point is where a start at 1.8 ended. It is lowest nearby, at $-1.0702$, but not lowest overall.

explain.text: Both points are local minima. The left one has $f \approx -3.5139$, below $-1.0702$, so it is global. A descent method finds whichever one its start leads to.

screens.title: One bowl
screens.prose: Now $f(x) = x^2$, which is convex. Drag the start anywhere along the curve, on either side.
screens.question: Where does the ball stop, whatever the start?

hints.text: Try a start on each side.
Every path ends at $x = 0$, the global minimum.

feedback.correct: Every start ends at 0. On a convex set, a local minimum of a convex function is global.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption for two or three starts.

byKey.start: That is the start. Read where the path ends.

explain.text: There is no second dip, so every descent ends at the global minimum. That is the theorem of this lesson: for a convex function on a convex set, local means global.

screens.title: The proof
screens.prose: Let $f$ be convex on a convex set $C$, and let $\mathbf{x} \in C$ be a local minimum. We show no point of $C$ is lower.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Leave out the lines that do not belong.

lines.text: For $0 < \theta \le 1$, $\mathbf{z} = \theta\mathbf{y} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{x}$ lies in $C$, because $C$ is convex.
Taking $\theta$ small puts $\mathbf{z}$ as close to $\mathbf{x}$ as we like, still with $f(\mathbf{z}) < f(\mathbf{x})$.
That contradicts local minimality, so no such $\mathbf{y}$ exists: $\mathbf{x}$ is a global minimum.
Since $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is the lowest point.
lines.why: The theorem assumes no derivative: $|x|$ has a global minimum at 0 with no gradient there.

lines.text: Since $f'' > 0$, the minimum is unique, so it is global.
lines.why: Convex does not give $f'' > 0$, and uniqueness is not the claim.

hints.text: It is a proof by contradiction: assume a lower point exists.
Walk from $\mathbf{x}$ towards $\mathbf{y}$; both convexities are used.
Points near $\mathbf{x}$ on that segment are lower than $\mathbf{x}$, which local minimality forbids.

feedback.correct: Assume a lower point, walk towards it, use both convexities, and points near $\mathbf{x}$ come out lower.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The set's convexity keeps $\mathbf{z}$ in $C$; the function's convexity makes it lower.

byKey.d1: That needs a derivative, and the theorem does not. The segment argument works without one.
byKey.d2: $f'' > 0$ is neither given nor needed. The claim is that a local minimum is global.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step: the assumption, the segment, the inequality, the limit or the contradiction.

explain.text: Convexity of $C$ keeps the segment inside, and convexity of $f$ puts the segment's values below the chord. So any lower point drags values below $f(\mathbf{x})$ arbitrarily close to $\mathbf{x}$.

screens.title: A flat bottom
screens.prose: Convex functions can have many minimisers. Take $g(x) = \max(|x| - 1, 0)$, a convex function with a flat floor.
screens.question: Which set of points minimises $g$?

options.why: You took the corners only. Every point between them also has $g = 0$.
You looked for a single bottom. The floor is flat from $-1$ to 1.

hints.text: So every point of $[-1, 1]$ is a minimiser.

feedback.correct: All of $[-1, 1]$. The set of minimisers of a convex function is convex: here an interval.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find every $x$ with $g(x) = 0$.

byKey.ends: The points between $-1$ and 1 also give 0.

explain.text: $g = 0$ on $[-1, 1]$ and positive outside. If two points minimise a convex function, the chord between them sits at the minimum value. So every point between does too.

screens.title: Gradient zero is enough
screens.prose: For a differentiable convex $f$, the tangent test gives $f(\mathbf{y}) \ge f(\mathbf{x}^*)$ when $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}$. So a stationary point is a global minimum. Take $f = x^2 + xy + y^2 - 3x$, with Hessian eigenvalues 1 and 3.
screens.question: Solve $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$. Give the global minimiser as a vector $(x, y)$.

feedback.correct: $(2, -1)$, with $f = -3$. Both eigenvalues are positive, so $f$ is strictly convex and this minimiser is the only one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set both partial derivatives to 0 and solve together.

byKey.xonly: You dropped the $xy$ term from $\partial f/\partial x$. With it, $2x + y = 3$ and $x + 2y = 0$.

explain.text: $2x + y = 3$ and $x + 2y = 0$ give $(2, -1)$, where $f = 4 - 2 + 1 - 6 = -3$. Strict convexity allows at most one minimiser, and the tangent test makes it global.

screens.title: A convex function on a gap
screens.prose: Minimise the convex $x^2$ over $[-3, -1] \cup [2, 4]$. A solver started at 3 slides down to 2 and stops: it cannot step into the gap. Both $x = -1$ and $x = 2$ are local minima on this set.
screens.question: Tap the global minimum.

hints.text: The global minimum is at $x = -1$, value 1.

feedback.correct: $x = -1$, value 1. The function is convex but the set is not, so the local minimum at 2 is not global.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two values.

byKey.local: You took the solver's answer. $f(2) = 4$, but $f(-1) = 1$ is lower: on a set with a gap, local is not global.

explain.text: $f(-1) = 1 < 4 = f(2)$. The theorem needs a convex set as well as a convex function. The segment from 2 to $-1$ leaves the set, so the proof breaks.

screens.title: No minimiser at all
screens.prose: Convexity says a local minimum is global. It does not promise one exists. Take $e^x$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
screens.question: Does $e^x$ attain a minimum on $\mathbb{R}$?

options.text: No: its values approach 0 as $x \to -\infty$ but never reach it.

options.why: $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$ is smaller, and so is every value further left.

options.text: Yes: every convex function has a global minimum.
options.why: Convexity makes a local minimum global, if there is one. $e^x$ has none.

feedback.correct: No minimiser: the infimum 0 is never attained. A solver keeps stepping left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a value lower than any you pick.

byKey.conv: The theorem is about a minimum that exists. Existence needs more, such as a closed bounded set.

explain.text: $e^x > 0$ for every $x$, and $e^x \to 0$ as $x \to -\infty$. So the infimum is 0 and no point attains it.

screens.title: Descent in code
screens.prose: Write `descend_1d(fprime, x0, s, n)`: take $n$ steps $x \leftarrow x - s f'(x)$ from `x0` and return the last $x$. Then `basins(fprime, starts, s, n)` returns each start's end point, rounded to 6 places. The hidden tests use `fq`, the derivative $4x^3 - 6x + 1$ of our quartic.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests in pure Python. Numbers and lists are compared with math.isclose, absolute tolerance 1e-9 where the expected value is 0 or rounded.

feedback.correct: Both pass. Starts $-2$, 0 and 0.16 end at $-1.30084$; starts 0.18 and 2 at 1.130901.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing row: it names the call and what came back.

explain.text: Starts either side of the hump at 0.1699 reach different minima. The answer depends on the start. On $x^2$ every start ends at 0 within $10^{-9}$.

screens.title: Why desks like convex models
screens.prose: A desk runs two optimisers. Model 1 minimises portfolio variance with a budget and long-only weights, a convex problem. Model 2 limits the book to ten names, which is not convex. Each returns a point where no small move improves the objective.

state.caption: Four starts of one nonconvex fit end at two different answers.

screens.question: What can the desk conclude?

options.text: Model 1's answer is the global optimum. Model 2's may be only local, and depends on the start.
Both answers are global, since no small move improves either.
options.why: No small move improving is local optimality. Only convexity upgrades it to global.

options.text: Neither can be trusted without many restarts.
options.why: Model 1 is convex: one run is certified. Restarts are for model 2, and even they certify nothing.

hints.text: Which model meets the theorem's two conditions?
Model 1: convex objective, convex set. Model 2: the set is not convex.
So model 1's local optimum is global; model 2's is not guaranteed.

feedback.correct: Whatever the convex solver returns is the answer. A nonconvex fit, such as a name limit or a network's loss, needs several starts. Even then it cannot be certified.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which model satisfies the theorem.

byKey.both: Local optimality is all a solver checks. Convexity is what makes it global.
byKey.neither: The convex model needs no restarts: its local optimum is global.

explain.text: Model 1 has a convex objective on a convex set, so its local optimum is global. Model 2's set is a union of pieces, one per choice of names. Different starts can then end at different answers, as the four paths show.

ideas: On a convex set, every local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum.
The set of minimisers is convex, and a strictly convex function has at most one. For differentiable convex $f$, $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ is enough.
Both conditions matter: $x^2$ on a set with a gap has a local minimum that is not global. And $e^x$ has no minimum at all.

formula.name: Local is global
formula.tex: f \text{ convex on convex } C,\ \mathbf{x} \text{ local min} \implies f(\mathbf{x}) \le f(\mathbf{y}) \ \forall \mathbf{y} \in C
formula.note: The proof walks from $\mathbf{x}$ towards any lower point.

summary.trap: A convex function on a nonconvex set can have a local minimum that is not global.

quiz.prose: A convex $f$ on a convex set $C$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{x}$, with $f(\mathbf{x}) = 3$.
quiz.question: What is the smallest value of $f$ on $C$?

feedback.correct: 3. On a convex set a local minimum of a convex function is global.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the theorem of this lesson.

byKey.zero: Nothing says $f$ reaches 0. The local minimum, 3, is the global one.

explain.text: Both convexity conditions hold, so the local minimum is global and the smallest value is 3.

quiz.question: How long is the interval of its minimisers?

feedback.correct: $h = 0$ exactly when $-2 \le x \le 1$, an interval of length 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where both $x - 1$ and $-2 - x$ are at most 0.

byKey.half: You halved the interval. It runs from $-2$ to 1.
byKey.one: You took only $[0, 1]$. The left end is $-2$.

explain.text: $x - 1 \le 0$ for $x \le 1$ and $-2 - x \le 0$ for $x \ge -2$. So $h = 0$ on $[-2, 1]$, length 3.

quiz.prose: A strictly convex $f$ has $f(\theta\mathbf{a} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{b}) < \theta f(\mathbf{a}) + (1 - \theta)f(\mathbf{b})$ for $\mathbf{a} \ne \mathbf{b}$ and $0 < \theta < 1$.
quiz.question: Can it have two different minimisers $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$?

options.text: No: the midpoint would be strictly lower than both.
Yes, if they have the same value.
options.why: Equal values are the case that fails: the midpoint is strictly below that common value.

options.text: Only on a set that is not convex.
options.why: On a convex set it is impossible; the midpoint is in the set.

feedback.correct: The midpoint would beat both, so at most one minimiser exists.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the strict inequality to the midpoint.

explain.text: If $f(\mathbf{a}) = f(\mathbf{b}) = m$ is the minimum, the midpoint has $f < m$. That contradicts $m$ being the minimum.
$f' = e^x - 2$ vanishes at $x = \ln 2 \approx 0.6931$. $f$ is convex, so this stationary point is the global minimum.
